prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks (B006) as my preferred single-part configuration after the full exchange. The discovery is one specific idea: trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the optical lattice does not shift the clock transition, which lets thousands of atoms be interrogated at once with neither Doppler nor recoil broadening. Katori proposed it and demonstrated it with strontium; Ye's group then showed that the lattice can be controlled and its many-body interactions understood well enough to reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. That has been reproduced and intercompared across JILA, Tokyo/RIKEN, PTB, SYRTE and others, so the result is not in doubt, and it is already used for gravitational redshift tests at the centimetre scale and for limits on varying constants and dark-sector couplings. The attribution is two names with a natural division between concept and record-setting demonstration, and I do not need a fourth or fifth name to make the citation true. I read the round-1 exchange as showing that all three leading ballots are scientifically sound, so the choice rests on maturity and attribution, and on those two criteria B006 is the least contested. I have not changed my preferred configuration. I have, however, tightened the citation to the lattice-clock concept and its demonstrated accuracy, with nothing about the frequency comb or ion clocks and nothing that depends on the redefinition of the second.
statement.case_against: The case remains a contestable one. Optical clocks have more than two fathers: ion-clock work (Wineland and others), comb technology honoured in 2005, and independent lattice work elsewhere, so a Katori-Ye prize draws a line through a communal achievement. Several colleagues (Mehlig, Eriksson, Olsson, Pearce) see precision improvement within a metrology line already recognised in 2005 and 2012, and I cannot prove that the novelty is large enough to answer them. Only two members preferred it, and a committee that ranked it fifth or sixth in the openings has not been moved by my arguments. I also have to weigh my own vantage as an atomic physicist, which may make me value the magic-wavelength idea more than colleagues from condensed matter would. Finally, if the committee takes the view that B025 or B013 is the more significant discovery in nature, B006 loses to them on breadth of consequence, even if it wins on cleanliness.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene as a clean prediction-then-discovery story that created a field, and in his round 1 reply to me he accepts that the Katori-Ye pairing is the cleanest attribution but doubts the novelty relative to the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I take the novelty objection seriously and answer it on content, not on counting. The 2005 prize honoured the comb as a way to count optical cycles and the 2012 prize honoured control of single quantum systems, in particular a single ion. Neither contains the magic-wavelength idea or the regime in which a large ensemble of neutral atoms is interrogated at once while the trapping field is made to cancel out, and that regime is what changed the statistical limit and led to 1e-18. I would call that a new method with a distinct physical principle, not a refinement of the same measurement. On B025, I accept that the experimental phenomenon is real and widely reproduced, and that is the strongest form of Mehlig's argument. My remaining difference is that the moire case needs the committee to be at ease with two attribution choices at once, Bistritzer against Andrei and the open pairing mechanism, whereas B006 needs neither.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B025 first for the Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction followed by Jarillo-Herrero's correlated insulating and superconducting states, argues that eight years of replication across moire platforms is enough, and names B013 and B006 as safer alternatives if the committee finds the field too fluid.
responses.response: I accept that the phenomenon at the magic angle is established, and that the chair's question is right to separate the secure core, correlated insulators and superconductivity, from the pairing mechanism. If the committee decides that the core is the credited discovery, my objection reduces to timing, and I would no longer call B025 scientifically doubtful. Where I still differ from Eriksson is on how the attribution question is closed. Naming Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero is defensible on the prediction-plus-discovery logic, but the citation then has to say that it concerns the magic-angle flat bands and the first correlated states, and that earlier scanning-probe evidence of flat-band signatures exists. I am glad to see Eriksson disclose his proximity to the subject; I disclose mine for B006 in the same spirit, and I would ask that the committee read both disclosures in the same way.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B013 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp and answered my round-1 position by saying that dropping Mele removes half of the original proposal of the spin Hall state and the Z2 invariant.
responses.response: I accept this and correct the record: the chair's summary carries forward my opening proposal of Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, but my round-1 preferred configuration is B006 and not B013. If the committee does choose topological insulators, I now think that Olsson and Danielsson are right that the defensible three-name set is Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, tied to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect. Hasan's three-dimensional work is a distinct achievement and including him by dropping Mele would invert the priority of the originating idea. So I withdraw my earlier Kane-Molenkamp-Hasan set and would vote for the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio if B013 were my configuration. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang remain a real omission that the citation cannot repair, and the 2016 prize overlap should be addressed in the citation text.

responses.point: Danielsson has moved from B033 to B013 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, restricts the citation to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect, and says that topological insulators have wider scientific consequence than a gain in precision while conceding that the clock case is cleaner on attribution.
responses.response: I agree that he is right to confine the citation to the two-dimensional case and not to bundle Xue's quantum anomalous Hall effect into it. On weight, I accept that a new organising principle for electronic matter has broader consequence than improved accuracy, and I do not claim that the clock is the more important idea in general. The prize criterion is a discovery of important benefit, and my judgement is that a clean two-name discovery with agreed credit and two decades of independent confirmation is the more defensible public position than a case whose credit is compound. I note that Danielsson's own argument about the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes would, if applied consistently, equally weigh the 2016 topology prize against B013, which is the field-neutral rule that the chair asked about.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads optical lattice clocks as a new discovery-plus-instrument advance or as continuation of the metrology line honoured in 2005 and 2012; I have given my reasons but the committee may weigh them differently.

Whether Katori and Ye fairly represent the origin of optical lattice clocks, given the ion-clock programmes and the independent lattice work at PTB, SYRTE and other Tokyo and JILA colleagues outside the credited names.

How heavily a committee should weigh the larger breadth of B025 and B013 against the attribution cleanliness of B006, and whether the 2016 topology prize and the 2025 circuits prize should lower B013 and B009 under a field-neutral rule.
For B025, whether the unresolved pairing mechanism and the Andrei priority question are a matter of timing only; I would revisit B025 as a clearly mature case in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: no documented collaboration or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or any other credited name on the shortlist; my collaborators (Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, Reinhold Schuch, J. Marcus Dahlstrom, Luca Argenti, Paul Indelicato) are not among them. As a theoretical atomic physicist I am subject-area close to B006 and B002, and I note that this proximity may bias me toward the clock case; I disclose it without treating it as a recusal ground, and I have tried to ask the same disclosure standard of Eriksson for B025. The chair's summary describes my set as Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, which was my opening proposal and is not my current position.
